subject: pathology
title: Thrombosis, embolism and infarction

steps.tx: Intravascular blood coagulation inside an intact living vessel defines **pathological thrombosis**, governed by Virchow triad: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability. Endothelial injury is the dominant driver of arterial thrombosis over ruptured atherosclerotic plaques, exposing subendothelial collagen to activate platelets. Stasis and turbulence disrupt laminar flow, promoting venous thrombosis in immobilized lower limbs. Primary hypercoagulability stems from mutations like factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A, whereas secondary hypercoagulability accompanies prolonged bed rest, malignancy, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
steps.say: Pathological thrombosis forms an inappropriate solid mass from blood constituents within the cardiovascular system. Rudolf Virchow identified three major influences that govern thrombus development: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability. Endothelial damage is paramount in arterial thrombosis, where plaque rupture triggers platelet adhesion and aggregation. Venous thrombosis is driven primarily by stasis and hypercoagulable states in the deep leg veins. Inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden mutation and acquired conditions like malignancy markedly increase venous clot risk.

steps.tx: Distinguishing an antemortem thrombus from a postmortem clot is an essential diagnostic skill in pathology. Thrombi formed in flowing blood display visible laminations termed **lines of Zahn**, representing alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin with darker erythrocyte-rich layers. These laminations demonstrate that the thrombus formed under hemodynamic shear forces. Thrombi are firm, friable, and firmly attached to the vascular endothelium. In contrast, postmortem blood clots are soft, gelatinous, rubbery, unattached to vessel walls, and settle into a dependent dark currant-jelly portion beneath a pale yellow chicken-fat layer.
steps.say: Differentiating a true antemortem thrombus from a postmortem clot is a fundamental skill in autopsy pathology. Thrombi formed in flowing blood exhibit characteristic lines of Zahn, consisting of alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin alongside darker layers of red blood cells. Furthermore, true thrombi are firm, friable and firmly anchored to the vessel wall. Postmortem clots form after cessation of flow and lack lines of Zahn. They are soft, rubbery, unattached to the endothelium, and separate into dark dependent blood beneath a yellow chicken fat layer.

left.title: Antemortem thrombus
points: Firm and attached to vessel wall

steps.tx: Microscopic examination of an **antemortem thrombus** demonstrates clear structural organization reflecting sequential hemodynamic deposition. Platelet-fibrin bands alternate with erythrocyte layers to construct classic lines of Zahn. Arterial thrombi tend to be non-occlusive mural thrombi in large vessels like the aorta, or occlusive in coronary arteries, growing in a retrograde direction toward the heart. Venous thrombi propagate in the direction of blood flow toward the heart, forming long, red, fibrin-rich cast-like tails in deep leg veins that are prone to fragmentation and downstream pulmonary embolization.
steps.say: Microscopic evaluation of an antemortem thrombus confirms that it was actively synthesized in flowing blood before death. The architecture reveals alternating lamellae of pale platelets and dense fibrin meshworks contrasting with darker trapped erythrocytes. Arterial thrombi typically begin at sites of endothelial erosion and propagate in a retrograde direction, often occluding coronary vessels to cause infarction. Venous thrombi arise in sluggish venous plexuses and grow in the direction of blood flow. Their loosely attached trailing red ends are exceedingly vulnerable to breaking loose as pulmonary emboli.

vis.caption: Comparison of an antemortem thrombus showing lines of Zahn and a postmortem clot.

steps.tx: Once established within a vessel, a thrombus evolves through propagation, embolization, dissolution, or **recanalisation**. In propagation, the thrombus accumulates additional platelets and fibrin, extending toward total occlusion. Embolization occurs when fragments detach and travel downstream to occlude distant capillary beds. Dissolution is mediated by fibrinolysis via plasmin, which is effective in freshly formed clots but ineffective in older cross-linked thrombi. Older thrombi undergo organization, where invading endothelial cells and fibroblasts convert the clot into vascularized connective tissue, creating new capillary channels that partially recanalise flow.
steps.say: Every thrombus follows one of four major physiological pathways: propagation, embolization, dissolution or organization with recanalisation. Fresh thrombi may propagate along the vessel lumen to produce total vascular occlusion, or fragments may break off as emboli to lodge distantly. Endogenous fibrinolysis can dissolve recent thrombi, but older clots become cross linked and refractory to lysis. In older thrombi, endothelial cells and fibroblasts invade the fibrin scaffold, organizing it into fibrous tissue. Within this fibrotic mass, newly formed vascular channels restore partial blood flow.

vis.alt: Four thrombus fates: propagation enlarges and may occlude; embolisation travels downstream and is the most dangerous early fate; dissolution by fibrinolysis works best on fresh clots; organisation brings fibrosis with recanalisation but resists lysis.
vis.caption: Fresh thrombi answer drugs; organised thrombi resist them.

steps.tx: The migration of detached intravascular physical material to a distant vascular bed defines **systemic embolism**, where the impacted embolus produces downstream ischemic occlusion. Greater than ninety-five percent of pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremities above the knee, ranging from silent microemboli to catastrophic saddle emboli causing sudden death. Systemic arterial emboli arise predominantly from intracardiac mural thrombi associated with myocardial infarction, dilated cardiomyopathy or atrial fibrillation, lodging downstream in the brain causing stroke, the mesenteric arteries causing bowel infarction, or lower extremity arteries causing gangrene.
steps.say: An embolus is any detached intravascular physical mass that is carried by the bloodstream to a distant site where it produces vascular occlusion. More than ninety percent of pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thrombosis in femoral or popliteal veins, lodging in pulmonary arteries to cause chest pain, infarction or sudden death. In contrast, systemic arterial emboli arise mainly from cardiac mural thrombi complicating myocardial infarction or atrial fibrillation. These arterial emboli travel downstream to cause catastrophic stroke in the brain, bowel infarction, or cold gangrene in the extremities.

steps.tx: Ischemic necrosis of parenchymal tissue caused by occlusion of arterial supply or venous drainage is termed an **infarct**. White or anemic infarcts occur with arterial occlusions in solid organs with end-arterial supply, like the heart, spleen and kidney, where tissue density limits hemorrhage into the necrotic zone. Red or hemorrhagic infarcts occur in venous occlusions, in loose tissues like the lung, and in dual-supply organs like intestines. Coagulative necrosis characterizes infarction in solid organs except the brain, where ischemia produces liquefactive necrosis.
steps.say: An infarct represents an area of localized ischemic tissue necrosis resulting from sudden interruption of arterial inflow or venous drainage. White anemic infarcts occur in solid organs with end arterial supply, such as the heart, kidneys and spleen, where tissue density limits blood extravasation into the necrotic zone. Red hemorrhagic infarcts occur in loose tissues like the lung, in organs with dual circulations, and following venous occlusion. Most infarcted tissues demonstrate classic coagulative necrosis with preserved cellular architecture, whereas cerebral infarction uniquely manifests as liquefactive necrosis.
